t: Minimum Prefix Removal to Make Array Strictly Increasing
o: We must delete a prefix so that what remains is strictly increasing; the best strategy keeps the longest strictly increasing suffix. In Example 1 the longest strictly increasing suffix is [3,4,5] starting at index 3, so we remove 4 elements. In Example 2 the suffix [-5] starts at index 3, so the answer is 3. In Example 3 the whole array is strictly increasing, so the suffix starts at index 0 and nothing is removed. With n up to 1e5, a single backward scan suffices.
k: The remaining array must be a suffix, so the answer is simply where the longest strictly increasing suffix begins.
One backward pass comparing adjacent elements solves it in O(n).

a.i: Walk from the right while each element is smaller than the one after it. The first index where this breaks (or 0) is the start of the longest strictly increasing suffix, which is exactly the prefix length to remove.
s: While i > 0 and nums[i-1] < nums[i], decrement i.
a.t: O(n) — single backward pass over the array.

a.n: Approach 2: Forward DP of increasing-run starts
a.i: Compute start[i] = the beginning index of the strictly increasing run ending at i (reset to i whenever nums[i] <= nums[i-1]). The answer is start[n-1], equivalent to the backward scan but derived forward.
s: For i from 1 to n-1: if nums[i] <= nums[i-1], set start = i.

w: Both approaches are equivalent; the backward scan is the most direct to explain. Key pitfall: strictness — equal adjacent elements force a cut (use <, not <=, when scanning backward). Edge cases: single-element arrays (answer 0) and arrays that are entirely non-increasing (answer n-1). Follow-up: what if you could remove any one contiguous subarray instead of a prefix?
